sections.h2: Who to call about a Lee County tax bill
sections.html:
Four offices in Dixon share the work. Questions about value or exemptions go to the assessment staff, payment problems go to the Treasurer, and questions about how a rate was figured go to the Clerk's extension department.

Lee County offices that touch a property tax bill
OfficeWhat it handlesPhone and location
Treasurer and CollectorPrints and collects bills, runs the annual tax sale, administers senior deferral815-288-4477, 112 E Second Street, mailing box 328
Chief County Assessment OfficeValues, exemptions, appeal paperwork815-288-4483, open weekdays from 8 until 4:30
Board of ReviewDecides assessment complaints815-288-4483, first floor of the old courthouse
County Clerk and RecorderExtends rates, takes redemption money after a sale, records deeds815-288-3309, mailing box 329

The Treasurer collects more than $96 million this year and passes it to over 130 taxing districts. That is why a Lee County bill reads like a ledger of school, township, fire and county lines instead of a single charge.

Population is 32,914 as of July 2025, down from 34,145 in 2020. About 73.6% of occupied homes have owners living in them. The midpoint value for an owner-occupied home is $154,600, and builders took out just 32 permits in 2025, so resale buyers have few new houses to compare against. Dixon is the seat and the biggest city. An EF4 tornado touched down in the county on April 9, 2015, so expect a buyer to ask about storm history.

Several school districts cut across the county, including Dixon Unit 170, Amboy 272, Ashton 275, Lee Center 271, Polo 222 and Sterling 5. Whichever one serves your address drives much of your rate.

sections.h2: How Lee County values a home
sections.html:
Township assessors propose values, and the county assessment office pulls them together. Houses are assessed at one-third of fair cash value. If a single parcel changes, the office mails you a notice. If the only change is a township-wide equalization factor, no notice is required.

Illinois runs on a four-year general reassessment. For 2026 the townships in their general year are Amboy, Ashton, Bradford, Franklin Grove, Nachusa, Lee Center, May and Sublette. You can look over a parcel's size, age, lot and sketch at the assessment counter, or search property record cards on the county site.

A bigger bill does not always mean a bigger assessment. Usually one of three things happened: a taxing district asked for more, an exemption you qualify for was never applied, or other owners picked up exemptions you lack. Under the state's extension limitation law, most districts may grow their levy by the smaller of 5% or inflation over the highest of the prior three years. New construction, bonds and referendum-approved increases sit outside that cap.

Put your complaint in writing and deliver it to the Board of Review inside 30 calendar days after the assessment list is published (35 ILCS 200/16-55). For the townships named above, the publication date is November 18, 2026 and the last day to file is December 18, 2026. Other townships have their own publication dates, so ask the assessment staff which one applies to you.

The Board has three members chosen by the County Board. It may confirm, lower or raise a value. These grounds are accepted:

  • Equity, meaning your value is out of line with similar homes
  • Fair cash value
  • A wrong physical description of the property
  • Questions of law

Before filing, try your township assessor or county staff, because many disputes are settled in that conversation. After the 30 days, only a physical-data mismatch, such as a house recorded larger than it is, can still be raised. If you dislike the Board's ruling, the Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board is the next step, at 217-782-6076 or 401 S Spring Street, Room 402, Springfield. It looks at value only, so a complaint about the size of the final bill belongs with the taxing districts.

sections.h2: Due dates and how to pay
sections.html:
The bill comes in two installments, and the county prints each due date on the bill. Under 35 ILCS 200/21-15, the first installment turns delinquent after the later of June 1 or the day following the printed date. The second follows the same test against September 1. Each month or part of a month that you are late adds interest of 1 1/2%. Mail with a postmark on or before the date is treated as timely.

Ways to pay:

  • The county's property tax inquiry website, which shows a pay link after you search by PIN, owner name or address.
  • Phone payment at 877-690-3729 with jurisdiction code 7042.
  • A check mailed to Lee County Collector, P.O. Box 328, Dixon, IL 61021.
  • The Treasurer's counter at the Old Lee County Courthouse.

Card payments carry a 2.40% fee through a third party, with a $2.00 minimum. E-checks cost $2 up to $50,000, then $4, $8.50 and $10 in higher bands. If you never got a bill, ask the Treasurer for a duplicate, because a missing bill does not cancel the debt. Send address updates on the county's change-of-address form.

Each exemption comes off your equalized assessed value ahead of the tax rate. Because no county with 3,000,000 or more residents touches Lee, the smaller statutory caps are the ones in force. Here are the common ones:

  • General homestead: up to $6,000 off a house you occupy as your main residence (35 ILCS 200/15-175).
  • Senior citizens: up to $5,000 off, starting in the assessment year you turn 65 (35 ILCS 200/15-170). Once approved it carries forward by itself, but you must notify the office if the home no longer qualifies.
  • Senior freeze: a yearly application, with household income kept under the limit on the county form.
  • Tax deferral: the Treasurer's program for owners 65 and over whose household income is at most $75,000, moving to $77,000 for tax year 2026 and $79,000 for 2027. The postponed tax stays as a lien until the house sells.

File exemption forms with the assessment office. After a sale, state law keeps the seller's homestead credit through the assessment year of the sale, and the office can ask the buyer to apply for the following year.

The thing auctioned at a tax sale is the delinquent tax, never the house itself. Each year the Treasurer puts every unpaid parcel into the sale. You keep the right to redeem by paying the tax plus added costs and interest, and the redemption desk is in the County Clerk's office.

State law usually allows three years from the sale date, with exceptions in 35 ILCS 200/21-350. If a buyer already holds a certificate on your parcel, get the Clerk's payoff figure and final date in writing before you set a price or sign a contract.

sections.h2: Property taxes at a Lee County closing
sections.html:
The title agent or closing attorney pulls the most recent bill, looks for open installments, and splits the tax year between you and the buyer on the settlement statement. Before that, ask the Treasurer whether any older year is delinquent or sold, since that balance must be cleared at the table. If a lender escrows your taxes, find out which installments it has already paid.

Houses that come with probate, tenants or deferred repairs often carry back taxes too. A payoff letter from the Treasurer, plus a redemption figure from the Clerk if a sale happened, lets you compare offers on equal terms. A cash buyer can close on whatever payoff figure those two offices give you, without waiting on a lender's tax review.

faqs.q: Which number reaches the Lee County Treasurer?
faqs.a: 815-288-4477 for bills and payments. The assessment office at 815-288-4483 takes value, exemption and appeal questions, and the Clerk's extension department at 815-288-3309 explains how rates are built and handles redemption.

faqs.q: Can I still appeal late in Lee County?
faqs.a: Only for a physical-data error, such as the wrong square footage on the record. Other complaints must come within 30 days of the roll's publication.

faqs.q: What is the largest general homestead reduction in Lee County?
faqs.a: $6,000 of equalized assessed value, because the county does not border one with 3,000,000 or more residents. The rule is 35 ILCS 200/15-175, and the assessment office takes the application.

faqs.q: What does late payment cost in Lee County?
faqs.a: Interest of 1 1/2% per month or partial month under 35 ILCS 200/21-15. The clock starts after the later of the statutory date or the day after the printed due date, and a timely postmark avoids it.

faqs.q: Does Lee County's senior deferral wipe out the tax?
faqs.a: No, it only delays it. The deferred amount becomes a lien and comes due when the house is sold. You must be 65 or older and apply through the Treasurer.
